---
title: "Unitizing"
---

Every coefficient in the [agreement chapter](agreement.qmd) assumes the
segments already line up, and only asks whether the categories match. That
assumption does a lot of work. This chapter is about the prior question: did
the coders mark the same stretches of text at all?

Established QDA software settles it with a single overlap threshold, yes or
no. What that discards is precisely the information about *how* the
boundaries differ.

## Getting the segments

```r
segments <- qda_segments(frag)
```

One list per coder, each a `{"start", "end", "value"}`. The positions come
from the export's position columns, which arrived with a later plugin
version: an older export raises rather than returning an empty result that
would read as total disagreement.

Only text sources give a continuum to measure boundaries on. PDF rectangles
do not, and they are dropped with a warning rather than quietly approximated
into character offsets.

## Krippendorff's unitizing alpha

```r
r <- qda_unitizing_alpha(segments)
r$alpha; r$Do; r$De
```

Like every alpha in the family, it is one minus a ratio of disorders,
observed against what chance would produce
[@Krippendorff2004ReliabilityContent]:

$$
{}_{u}\alpha \;=\; 1 - \frac{{}_{u}D_o}{{}_{u}D_e},
$$

with

- ${}_{u}D_o$ — the disorder observed on the continuum,
- ${}_{u}D_e$ — the disorder expected for randomly placed units.

Here the disorder is measured on the *continuum*: for every pair of
coders, overlapping units are compared by the squared distance between their
boundaries, and what one coder marked while the other left a gap enters with
its full squared length. ${}_{u}D_e$ is the same quantity for units placed at
random on a continuum of the same length. (The defining paper, Krippendorff
1995, *On the Reliability of Unitizing Continuous Data*, is on the
[literature page](../dev/literature.qmd) and will be citable here once it is
in the library.)

Chance-corrected, and it treats a continuum of coded units and gaps. Two
coders agreeing that a stretch is irrelevant is *not* counted as evidence of
reliable unitizing, which is what separates this from the category-level
alpha.

Passing `metric=lambda a, b: 0` measures identification alone, ignoring the
codes. Do not expect that to raise alpha as a rule: it lowers the observed
disagreement, but it lowers the expected one too, because randomly paired
units no longer differ by category either. Where the coders disagreed about
categories, alpha rises; where they agreed throughout, it falls. Compare the
two `Do` values rather than the two alphas.

## WindowDiff and Pk

```r
qda_window_diff(ref, hyp, length_)
qda_pk(ref, hyp, length_)
```

Two error rates from text segmentation, reported together because they
disagree informatively. Both slide a window of width $k$ along the continuum
and count the positions where reference and hypothesis disagree about the
window's interior; WindowDiff compares the *number* of boundaries inside it:

$$
\text{WD} \;=\; \frac{1}{N-k}\sum_{i=1}^{N-k}
\mathbf{1}\!\left[\, b_{\text{ref}}(i, i{+}k) \neq b_{\text{hyp}}(i, i{+}k) \,\right],
$$

with

- $N$ — the length of the continuum,
- $k$ — the width of the sliding window,
- $b_{\text{ref}}$, $b_{\text{hyp}}$ — the number of boundaries the
  reference and the hypothesis place inside the window,
- $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ — one where the two disagree, zero otherwise.

Pk only asks whether the window's two ends fall in the same segment or
not. A spurious extra boundary therefore costs something in the first and
nothing in the second.

Neither is chance-corrected. What they offer instead is comparability with
the segmentation literature and sensible behaviour on near misses: a boundary
two characters off is nearly right, and both say so. (Their defining papers,
Pevzner & Hearst 2002 and Beeferman et al. 1999, are on the
[literature page](../dev/literature.qmd).)

## Gamma

```r
g <- qda_gamma(segments)
g$gamma; g$alignment
```

Gamma refuses to separate the two questions [@Mathet2015UnifiedHolistic].
Rather than measuring agreement on a fixed alignment, it searches for the
pairing of units across coders that minimises a combined positional and
categorical disorder $\delta$, and reports agreement with respect to that
best alignment:

$$
\gamma \;=\; 1 - \frac{\delta_{\text{observed}}}{\delta_{\text{expected}}},
$$

with

- $\delta_{\text{observed}}$ — the combined positional and categorical
  disorder of the best alignment,
- $\delta_{\text{expected}}$ — the same quantity from re-running the
  search on random continua.

Unitizing and categorisation are judged together.

The practical difference from the unitizing alpha: gamma can pair two units
that do not overlap at all, when the surrounding configuration says they
refer to the same phenomenon. Alpha cannot express that.

::: {.callout-warning title="Gamma is exact or it is nothing"}

Finding the best alignment is a set-partitioning problem, NP-hard for
three or more coders. This implementation searches exhaustively with the
paper's pruning rule and an admissible bound. When the search would
exceed `max_nodes` it returns `nan` with a reason rather than the best
thing it happened to find, because a gamma produced by a heuristic is not
gamma. If that happens, raise the budget or analyse a smaller stretch.
:::

Chance correction is by sampling, so `samples` and `seed` matter and the
result carries `recommended_samples`: how many random continua the observed
variability suggests for two per cent precision. If that exceeds what you
ran, run it again with more.

## Which one to report

Report the unitizing alpha when your question is whether the coders agreed on
*where* the relevant material is, and gamma when you want one number for the
whole job of unitizing and coding [@Mathet2015UnifiedHolistic]. WindowDiff
and Pk are worth adding when your audience knows the segmentation
literature. Sources are on the [literature page](../dev/literature.qmd).
